question: Housing costs, arrears and displacement pressure are on the rise in a number of Member States. Even food bank charity ‘Die Tafel Österreich’ has spoken in a broadcast of the plight affecting many families.

Meanwhile, at EU level, there is still no uniform, comparable body of data on evictions, while regulatory and energy policy requirements can drive construction and renovation costs even higher and exacerbate supply shortages. Given these circumstances, clear information is clearly needed on data, EU funds and the structural conditions that are driving up prices. 1.

What EU-wide comparable data does the Commission currently have on evictions, what gaps are there in that data, and when does the Commission plan to introduce standardised monitoring of the situation – including key variables such as eviction notices vs. enforcement, the main reasons and a breakdown by region?

What EU funds – broken down by programme and year – have been made available and disbursed since 2021 to address the housing crisis and prevent evictions, and to what extent does the EU directly support housing-related social benefits, such as rent subsidies or similar instruments?

What does the Commission make of the impact of regulation density, authorisation and reporting requirements and energy and climate policy requirements on construction and renovation costs, supply shortages and rent levels, particularly given the strained economic situation, and what remedial measures does it see as a priority?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.5.2026) Data on evictions are collected, analysed and disseminated by national authorities in the Member States. Any potential future developments at EU level in this regard would need to meet the core quality requirements1.

The Affordable Housing Database2 developed by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development includes data on evictions, however it has several limitations, related to different stages of an eviction process, timing of data collection, uneven coverage of jurisdictions, and gaps regarding mortgage foreclosures.

The Commission is advancing the implementation of the European Affordable Housing Plan (EAHP)3, and as part of the actions thereof, seeks to identify successful models and best practices that align property rights protection with tenant security. Regarding EU funds available for housing, at least EUR 45 billion have been mobilised in housing related investment4.

Overall, it is challenging to get more granular data per year on disbursement of funds given that no granular data collection on housing, nor on evictions, is available under the existing reporting setup.

Housing supply is subject to many rules at various levels – most rules being set at Member State, regional or local level – which aim to preserve safety and quality of life, promote social and economic objectives, and protect environment and cultural heritage.

But too often they lead to unnecessary administrative complexity resulting in unnecessary costs and delays, restricting the supply of housing where it is most needed. As announced in the EAHP, the Commission will contribute to cutting red tape to facilitate the supply of affordable and sustainable housing where it is most needed by presenting a housing simplification package in 2027.
